title: She Moved In as a Dependent at 62. Here’s How Much She Could Get Based on Her Daughter’s Social Security Record.
summary: Surviving parents may qualify for benefits only if their adult children provided half of their support. Here's how much a parent can get.
body_markdown:
Moving in with an adult child at 62 does not qualify a parent for Social Security based on the work record of that family member. Benefits for parents are available only after the son or daughter dies, and only if the parent received at least half of their support from them. Here is what a surviving parent could get, how to document that support and other benefits that may be available before then.


## When a Senior Parent Can Qualify for Benefits Through a Child


Social Security treats payments to parents as a[type of survivor benefit](https://smartasset.com/retirement/things-to-know-about-social-security-survivor-benefits) , so the work history of the supporting adult child and the finances of the family both matter.1 The adult child must have been fully insured when they died, meaning they had earned enough work credits for their age. The parent must be at least 62, meet the Social Security definition of a parent and file an application.2


The support test is usually the hardest requirement to prove.[Social Security](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-calculator) weighs housing, food, medical care and other costs the adult child covered against all support the parent received, including their own income. If the adult child was disabled before they died, the test may apply to the date their disability began rather than their date of death.


[Claiming a parent as a dependent](https://smartasset.com/financial-advisor/tax-implications-of-parent-living-with-you) on a tax return or letting them live with an adult child doesn’t satisfy the test by itself. The parent generally must submit proof within two years of the child’s death. If support is measured at the start of the child’s disability, the deadline is generally two years after the disability application. Social Security can extend these deadlines for good cause. The table breaks down the requirements:


Requirement What It Means How to Show It


Adult child was fully insured They earned enough work credits for their age before they died Social Security earnings record of the adult child


Parent is at least 62 The parent can’t claim before 62 Birth certificate or other proof of age


Parent relationship Biological parent, adoptive parent who adopted before the adult child turned 16 or stepparent who married into the family before the adult child turned 16 Birth, adoption or marriage records


Adult child provided at least half of support Measured at death, or when a qualifying disability began Records of rent, groceries, medical bills and other expenses the adult child paid


Proof filed on time Generally within two years of the death Signed support statement and supporting documents


No remarriage The parent hasn’t married since the death Marital records


No larger amount of their own The parent can’t already qualify for a retirement payment equal to or higher than the survivor amount[Social Security earnings record](https://smartasset.com/retirement/will-doubling-earnings-double-social-security-here-is-how-much-75k-and-150k-salaries-may-collect) of the parent


If you move in with an adult child at 62, tracking expenses from the start could help show support should they later cover at least half of your costs. Keeping receipts and payment records would make that easier to prove when you file a claim. A[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=shemovedinasdependentat62hereishowmuchshecouldgetbasedondaughtersocialsecurityrecord_a) can help you assess how this arrangement affects your retirement income and expenses.


## How Much a Senior Parent Could Get Through a Child


To show how this works, let’s assume that your daughter had a $3,000[primary insurance amount (PIA)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-social-security-benefit-based-on) , which is the figure Social Security uses to calculate payments on her work record. If you are the only parent entitled, you would receive 82.5% of that amount.3 This works out to $2,475 per month ($3,000 × 0.825). Unlike most other survivor payments, the benefit isn’t reduced for claiming at 62. The 82.5% rate is the same whether you start at 62, 65 or 67, although the amount actually payable may still be affected by other[Social Security rules](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-eligibility) .


If two parents qualify on the same record, each receives 75% instead, and the combined total can’t exceed the family maximum set for the earnings of the adult child. A parent who already qualifies for a smaller[retirement payment](https://smartasset.com/retirement/retired-at-63-tapping-our-401k-before-social-security-changed-everything) of their own would receive that amount first, plus the difference needed to reach the survivor figure. The table below compares the monthly and annual payments under each example, assuming no other[benefit adjustments](https://smartasset.com/retirement/social-security-early-retirement-penalty-chart) .


Example Calculation Monthly Payment Annual Payment


One parent qualifies $3,000 × 82.5% $2,475 $29,700 ($2,475 × 12)


Two parents qualify $3,000 × 75% for each parent $2,250 each, or $4,500 combined $27,000 each, or $54,000 combined


One parent with a $1,200 retirement payment of her own $1,200 + ($2,475 − $1,200) $2,475 total ($1,200 own + $1,275 survivor) $29,700


As the parent in the example, the record you build while living with your daughter matters more than the age when you claim survivor benefits, because these payments are not reduced for starting at 62. However, the amount you receive could still be affected by the family maximum or your own[retirement benefits](https://smartasset.com/retirement/retirement-calculator) .


## Other Programs That Could Help Support Senior Parents


[Supplemental Security Income (SSI)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/ssi-benefits) pays a monthly amount to adults 65 and older with limited income and assets, regardless of anyone else’s work record. Free housing from an adult child can lower that payment, but free meals do not reduce SSI benefits under rules effective since September 30, 2024, so the living arrangement affects how much a parent receives.4


[Medicaid](https://smartasset.com/insurance/who-qualifies-for-medicaid) may also cover medical and[long-term care costs](https://smartasset.com/insurance/how-much-does-long-term-care-insurance-cost) for parents who meet state income and asset limits, while[Medicare Savings Programs](https://smartasset.com/retirement/medicare-savings-programs) can pay[Medicare premiums](https://smartasset.com/retirement/medicare-premium-cost-2024-expect-to-pay) and, in some cases, deductibles and copays.


Families caring for an older parent can also turn to the National Family Caregiver Support Program, which offers respite care, training and counseling through local area agencies on aging.5


For housing costs, the Section 202 program from the Department of Housing and Urban Development supports affordable rental housing for low-income seniors.6 Separately, the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) might also help with heating and cooling bills.7


**Whether you are a parent or adult child, a[financial advisor](https://smartasset.com/retirement/find-a-financial-planner?utm_source=smartasset&utm_medium=google_discover_referral&utm_campaign=dp_social_security&utm_content=shemovedinasdependentat62hereishowmuchshecouldgetbasedondaughtersocialsecurityrecord_a) can help you understand how these programs may affect your retirement income and expenses.**
